proposition: Stop offering tax reductions or cash payments to individual companies in exchange for locating or expanding here.
yesMeans: Ends deals that cut taxes or pay grants to individual companies.
noMeans: Keeps deals that cut taxes or pay grants to individual companies.
scope: Every level in the issue's current mask can act. City and county: Chapter 380/381 agreements, tax abatements, TIF-funded grants. State: deal-closing funds and statutory abatements. Federal: firm-specific credits, subsidies, and siting deals. School district: Texas boards vote on property-value limitation agreements with individual companies under the 2023 HB 5 program (Chapter 403), so a trustee genuinely casts this vote — it is not a manufactured silence.
changedBecause: All three reviewers passed it unchanged.

proposition: Limit how much landlords can raise the rent each year on current tenants.
yesMeans: The yearly increase is capped by law for a tenant who stays.
noMeans: The yearly increase is set at lease renewal, with no legal cap.
scope: State and local, where most rent regulation sits: cities and counties adopt caps, and states either authorize them or preempt local authority. Federal action is narrow, reaching mainly federally subsidized or financed housing.
changedBecause: Stem unchanged — both partisan reviewers cleared it, and the overlap reviewer confirmed no duplication with the zoning item (price on existing units vs. what may be built), so no move to new ground was needed. Both glosses rewritten. "Ceiling" became "cap": it matches the stem's own verb and drops the price-ceiling textbook association the left reviewer flagged. Dropped "themselves" from the disagree gloss — the one clear tilt in the draft, flagged by both sides, since it described the status quo as one party acting unilaterally rather than as a renewal term. Gave the disagree side affirmative content ("set at lease renewal") instead of pure negation, per the right reviewer. Declined that reviewer's longer version, "whatever a landlord asks and a tenant agrees to at renewal" — "agrees to" imports the contract-and-competition rationale, which is an argument for that answer rather than a description of it, and at 15 words against the agree gloss's 11 it breaks the symmetry the format requires. Kept "current tenants": both reviewers independently defended it as precision, since removing it would silently ask about vacancy control instead. Both glosses now share a subject and structure ("The yearly increase is…") at equal length, so neither reads as the affirmative option.

proposition: Raise tax rates or create new taxes, so this government takes in more money than it does today.
yesMeans: Tax rates rise or new taxes begin, and the government takes in more.
noMeans: Tax rates hold or fall, and the government takes in the same or less.
scope: All levels. City, county, school district, and other special districts set rates and levies; states set income, sales, and business taxes; Congress sets federal rates and creates new taxes. The proposition always refers to the taxing body the office serves, and the guide should render that body's name (city, county, district, state, federal) alongside the question.
changedBecause:
Accepted the strongest critique, made by both reviewers: "total tax revenue" is not an action an officeholder takes. Property revenue climbs on its own with appraisals and new construction, so an incumbent who never voted a rate increase would score as a yes while the voter answering the same question meant a deliberate tax increase. The proposition now names the mechanism — raise rates or create new taxes — which is the thing that actually appears on an agenda or a floor vote, and the "takes in more money than it does today" clause fixes the direction and the baseline.

Accepted the parallelism complaint but not either reviewer's fix. "Budget within it" did carry a fiscal-discipline virtue frame, and the left reviewer was right that "fund a larger budget" answers it with a size-of-government frame rather than an equivalent. But their repair keeps spending in both glosses, and the plain reviewer showed why that is wrong: the proposition asks about taxing, not spending, so a candidate who wants more revenue to close a deficit, rebuild reserves, or pay down debt agrees with the sentence and disagrees with the gloss. Both glosses now stay on the tax side only, use the same verb pair (rise/hold, begin/fall), and carry no virtue word in either direction.

Dropped "rather than holding it at or below the current level." It restated the no answer inside the question, which is what the glosses are for, and cost seven words against the one-read test.

Rejected the plain reviewer's "this city." It fails the multi-level requirement outright — the same proposition has to serve a school board race and a Senate race — so "this government" stays, with the vagueness handled in scope by naming the body next to the question rather than by hardcoding one level into the wording. Also rejected their bare "Raise taxes": it reads as a slogan and reopens the rate-versus-revenue ambiguity their own critique identified.

Left unfixed on purpose: "hold flat" and "cut" still share the no side. That is inherent to a binary, and the noMeans states both outcomes plainly so nobody is misled about what they checked. If the taxonomy has room, a separate proposition on cutting taxes below today's level is the right way to split those two camps — not a three-way answer here.

Fairness test: a candidate running on a tax cut reads this and says yes, that is the choice, and I am a no. A candidate running on a bond-and-levy platform reads it and says yes, that is the choice, and I am a yes. Neither answer is dressed as the responsible one.

proposition: Increase public funding for K-12 schools above current levels, even if that requires raising taxes.
yesMeans: School funding should go up, and raising taxes is an acceptable way to pay for it.
noMeans: School funding should not go up if raising taxes is what pays for it.
scope: All levels, with different levers. School boards and districts set local budgets and place levies or bonds on the ballot; states carry the largest share through school-aid formulas, appropriations, and state taxes; Congress sets federal programs such as Title I and IDEA. Read it as the funding and taxes the office in question actually controls.
changedBecause: Both the conservative and plain reviewers independently found the same real defect, and they were right: the old "disagreeing means" added a commitment the item never asked about. A candidate who wants more school money from reallocation instead of new taxes must answer no, and was then printed as favoring flat funding. Only one side got an extra position attached. Both glosses are now exact complements on the trade-off, matched in length. I did not adopt the reviewers' replacement no-gloss, which ran two to three times the length of the yes-gloss — that is asymmetry of a different kind, and the extra clause explaining what a no does not mean belongs in the guide's method note, not in the answer label. The proposition itself is unchanged: both reviewers said the tax clause is fair and that deleting it would tilt the item toward yes by making the money look free. Rejected naming a specific government in the stem — that breaks the many-offices rule and is handled in scope — and rejected pinning "above current levels" to per-pupil or inflation-adjusted dollars, which narrows the choice and adds jargon a voter would have to decode.

proposition: Use public funds to cover the full tuition of in-state students at public colleges and universities.
yesMeans: Public funds pay tuition; students still cover fees, housing, and books.
noMeans: Students cover tuition themselves, through savings, family, financial aid, or loans.
scope: Primarily state: legislatures and governors set public college appropriations and tuition. Federal officials can act through matching or grant programs; locally elected community college district boards set their own tuition. Not actionable by city councils or county boards.
changedBecause: Accepted three critiques. (1) Both reviewers flagged "public funds go elsewhere" in the no gloss: a no does not entail redirecting the money, and a common reason to disagree is not appropriating it at all. The no gloss now says only who pays tuition under the status quo, inventing no destination. (2) Accepted the tuition-vs-total-cost trap. "Students pay none" read as "college is free" when tuition is often under half the bill. The yes gloss now names what stays unpaid — fees, housing, books — so a voter knows what they are agreeing to. (3) Changed "eliminate tuition" to "cover the full tuition" so the stem describes the mechanism (public money paying an existing charge) rather than the charge vanishing; "full" keeps it a change from today's partial aid rather than a restatement of it. Rejected the claim that the old glosses read as benefit-vs-harm and needed a cost added to the yes side: the cost is now on the yes side (remaining fees, housing, books) and the stem names the funding source, but I did not add a tax or spending consequence, which would have loaded the yes side against itself. Rejected the split into community college versus four-year propositions. It is a real distinction, but the format is one proposition per issue, and a candidate who backs only free community college registers a legible disagreement with the universal version — that is the proposition doing its job, not a defect. Kept "in-state students": it is load-bearing (it is the residency line every state already draws) and widely understood. Kept the stem silent on level of government; scope carries that.

proposition: Expand who qualifies for government-funded health coverage such as Medicaid.
yesMeans: More people qualify for government-funded coverage, and public spending on it goes up.
noMeans: The same number or fewer qualify, and public spending on it holds or falls.
scope: Federal and state. Congress sets Medicaid's core rules and match rate; states choose optional eligibility levels, waivers, and enrollment rules. Cities and counties act only where they fund their own clinics or local coverage programs.
changedBecause:
Accepted, because all three reviewers landed on it independently: dropped the trailing clause "so more people are covered than today." It stated a contested causal claim (eligibility is not enrollment) as settled, and it gave the yes side a stated purpose the no side never got. "Expand" already carries the direction and the baseline, so nothing is lost.

Accepted: fixed the internal contradiction. "Keep or narrow who qualifies" paired with "hold spending where it is" was incoherent — tightening eligibility lowers spending. Both branches now carry a matching two-part range: eligibility direction plus spending direction, open-ended up on one side, same-or-down on the other. That also cures the left reviewer's real complaint (a price tag on only one branch) without importing a consequence claim.

Accepted: made the stem and glosses use one term. Now "government-funded coverage" throughout. Rejected the left reviewer's preference for "public coverage" on polling grounds — "government-funded" is the more literal, mechanical description of the mechanism (where the money comes from), and the right reviewer independently read it as the phrasing that disfavors the yes side, which is evidence it is not a partisan term.

Rejected the left reviewer's proposed noMeans, "the number of people without coverage stays the same or grows." That restores the same contested causal claim the stem just shed, and does it as a harm attached to one branch only. A gloss that tells a voter what disagreement costs in uninsured people, while the agree branch names only gains, is the mirror image of the tilt being complained about.

Rejected the plain reviewer's stem, "More people should qualify ... even though covering them costs more public money." "Should" plus a concession clause argues the case rather than naming the change, and it fails the mechanism rule.

Rejected the plain reviewer's request to strip rollback out of the no side and keep it as pure status quo. Disagreeing with an expansion honestly spans "leave it alone" and "tighten it," both are positions real candidates run on, and the range is stated plainly rather than hidden. Splitting them off would leave candidates who want less spending with no fair place to land on this question.

proposition: Make abortion legal in more circumstances than the law in this jurisdiction now allows.
yesMeans: Abortion becomes legal in more circumstances than it is today.
noMeans: Abortion stays legal in the same circumstances as today, or fewer.
scope: State and federal only, matching the STATE_UP level mask already on this issue in packages/db/src/seed.ts. State legislatures and governors write most of the law on when abortion is legal; Congress, federal agencies, and the courts set national rules, funding conditions, and drug approval. City councils, county offices, and school boards do not set legality — their reach is limited to spending, enforcement priority, and clinic siting — so the proposition is not offered for those offices.
changedBecause: All three reviewers passed it unchanged.

proposition: Increase funding for police departments above current levels.
yesMeans: Police departments receive more funding than they receive now.
noMeans: Police departments receive the same funding as now, or less.
scope: All levels, each acting on the budget it controls: city council and mayor over a municipal police budget; county board and sheriff over a county force; state legislature and governor over state police and grants to local departments; Congress over federal grant programs to state and local police. Record a candidate against the budget their office actually votes on.
changedBecause: Accepted the shared objection to "the money government spends on police departments" and replaced it with "funding for police departments." Two reviewers landed on it independently, the guide already uses "funding" for the parallel health item (packages/db/src/seed.ts:89), and the spending frame activated fiscal-restraint priors against the answer it labeled while also leaving the actor vague. Rejected the request to drop "above current levels" as redundant, which both reviewers made. "Increase" alone floats its baseline: a candidate promising an increase over a proposed cut, or over last year's reduced budget, would read as a yes while still funding below today's level. The clause pins the comparison to the current budget for both the extractor and the voter, and it costs one short phrase. Rewrote both glosses to be strict restatements of the stem with matched length and no consequence language. Did not try to unbundle "flat or smaller" on the no side, which all three reviewers raised: it is the true complement of the stem, and splitting it would need a three-way answer the stance field does not have. A candidate defending the current budget and one proposing cuts do record identically, and the distinction belongs in the position summary, not in a reworded stem. Rejected adding an inflation baseline ("in real dollars"). Candidates almost never speak that way, so it would push most sources into NO_STATED_POSITION and add jargon that fails the one-read test. Rejected "should" phrasing, which turns the item into an opinion poll rather than a policy change. Left the jurisdiction out of the voter-facing sentence and put it in scope, since naming a level would break the item for offices at other levels.

proposition: Stop using money bail as a condition of releasing people before trial.
yesMeans: Courts decide pretrial release using conditions other than money bail.
noMeans: Courts decide pretrial release using money bail among other conditions.
scope: Mainly state and county: state legislatures write bail law, judges and magistrates apply it, and prosecutors and sheriffs shape practice. Congress sets it for federal courts only. Municipal offices have little direct lever.
changedBecause:
Accepted the plain reviewer's central point: the draft was double-barreled, bundling how many people get released with whether money is the mechanism. New Jersey and Illinois show these come apart — end cash bail while detaining more people outright — and that candidate had no home in the old wording. The proposition now fixes only the mechanism, and says nothing about the number released, which also removes the baseline-free "more."

Accepted the right reviewer's two smaller points. Register is now consistent ("people before trial" in both the stem and the glosses; "defendants" is gone), and the glosses are parallel: same verb, same structure, differing only in whether money bail is among the conditions, so neither side is the one merely "keeping" something.

Rejected the right reviewer's core claim that "money payment" is reform framing and the wording should be "refundable security" or "surety bond." That reviewer conceded in the same breath that "money bail" is statutory language both sides use; switching to bond-industry vocabulary would tilt the other way. Also rejected their suggested rewrite: "should require money bail less often" reintroduces the frequency question the plain reviewer just showed is a separate proposition, and has no baseline.

Rejected the plain reviewer's implied fix of softening to a partial reform. An absolute stem is what makes this answerable yes or no, and it matches how the choice actually presents itself to officeholders — a state either uses money bail or does not. The scope note now says plainly that this is thin for city races.

proposition: Require a background check on every gun sale, including sales between private individuals.
yesMeans: Private sales between individuals would require a background check.
noMeans: Private sales between individuals would not require a background check.
scope: Federal and state. Congress sets the baseline check requirement for licensed dealers; states can extend it to private sales, and roughly twenty have. Cities and counties are preempted from firearm sales rules in most states, so local offices act on this only in the minority of states without preemption.
changedBecause: Adopted the gloss fix, which both the conservative and the ordinary-voter reviewer reached independently: "would stay exempt from" is not the negation of "would also require." "Exempt" implies a carve-out from a rule the seller was inside, which is a description of current federal law that only one side would write. The pair now differs only by "not," so neither answer carries connotation the other lacks. Rejected the broadening from "sale" to "transfer." The plain reviewer is right that real bills usually say transfer and that gifts, inheritance, and lending are unresolved here, but "transfer" is drafting jargon a voter does not parse on one read, and quietly swapping it in would change what candidates are being scored against without saying so. The narrower sentence is the honest one; gifts and loans, if wanted, are a separate proposition. Rejected adding the operational mechanism ("through a licensed dealer," a fee, a waiting period). Naming one implementation would make the yes answer a specific bill rather than the policy direction, and candidates who back the requirement while differing on routing would be scored as opposed. "Background check" is already the mechanism; the rule against goals is satisfied. Kept the proposition despite the reviewer's point that it polls around 85-90 percent agree among the public. The measure exists to separate candidates, not to split the electorate, and on that it still divides cleanly. Added "sales between private individuals" in place of "private sales between individuals" for readability; no change in meaning.

proposition: Allow people now living in the United States without legal status to become permanent legal residents (green card holders).
yesMeans: People here without legal status become eligible for permanent residency.
noMeans: People here without legal status remain ineligible for permanent residency.
scope: Federal only. Congress writes immigration status law and the President signs or vetoes it. Governors, mayors, county commissioners, and school boards cannot change who is eligible for permanent residency, so this proposition should be run on federal races and not scored down-ballot. State and local immigration items (police cooperation with federal agents, in-state tuition, local ID cards, detention contracts) are separate propositions.
changedBecause:
The right and plain reviewers independently found the same defect and they are correct: the old sentence was double-barreled. "Without first leaving the country" bundled two decisions — is there any route to permanent residency, and if so must you file from abroad — so a candidate who opposes any route and a candidate who wants touchback processing both landed on "disagree" for opposite reasons, and the old noMeans silently credited restrictionists with backing a pathway they reject.

I rejected the fix both of them proposed. Widening noMeans into a compound ("either because they should leave and apply from abroad, or because there should be no path at all") papers over the problem: a "disagree" cell that means two incompatible things tells a voter nothing, which defeats the side-by-side comparison the guide exists for. The honest repair is to put the single live decision on the ballot and drop the procedural rider. That also fixes the plain reviewer's usability point — adjustment of status versus consular processing is a mechanism almost no candidate speaks to, so the old wording would have returned NO_STATED_POSITION for nearly everyone while voters answered the bigger question they thought they were asked. If the guide later wants the filing-location question, it is a second proposition, asked only of candidates who answer yes here.

Kept over objection: "people living in the United States without legal status" (the right reviewer explicitly blessed it, and "undocumented" is one side's term), and "become permanent legal residents" rather than "apply for" — "apply for" sounds conditional and makes the yes side cheaper to agree with. Adopted from the plain reviewer: "(green card holders)" as a plain-language gloss, so readers do not answer as if the question were citizenship and voting rights, while the precise term stays in the sentence. Dropped "first" as the right reviewer asked — it presumed the residency was coming — along with the whole clause it sat in.

Glosses rewritten to be symmetric in kind, answering the right reviewer's "principle versus paperwork" complaint: both are now the same ten-word eligibility statement with the direction flipped, so neither side gets an argument the other does not.

Left reviewer filed nothing.

proposition: Require electric utilities to stop generating electricity from fossil fuels by a deadline set in law.
yesMeans: A date set in law by which utilities must stop fossil fuel generation.
noMeans: No date set in law; utilities decide their own timing.
scope: Federal and state offices, where clean-electricity standards and utility rules are actually set. Also county and city offices that own a municipal utility or public power district. Not school boards, and not city or county offices with no utility authority — the current NOT_SCHOOL level list is too broad for this proposition.
changedBecause: Accepted three critiques both reviewers raised independently. (1) "government-set" went to "set in law": "Require" already establishes that a government imposes the rule, so the second mention added framing, not information, and "government-mandated/-imposed" is one side's vocabulary. "Set in law" keeps the load-bearing fact — the deadline is binding, not voluntary — which is the actual axis of disagreement, so I did not simply delete the modifier. (2) Fixed the garden path: "phase out power from fossil fuels" reads for a beat as "phase out power." "Stop generating electricity from fossil fuels" parses on one pass. (3) Rewrote both glosses onto one axis — whether a legal end date exists and who therefore sets the timing. The old pair was asymmetric: agreeing was glossed only as who imposes ("Government sets the deadline"), disagreeing as autonomy ("choose their own mix of fuels"), which handed the no side a benefit the yes side never got and widened the no side past the proposition into general utility discretion. Rejected the left reviewer's "applies to every utility" in the yes gloss — universal coverage is a separate design choice the proposition does not make. Rejected the plain reviewer's "utilities decide when, or whether, to stop": "or whether" is true under no mandate but makes the no side sound like never, a tilt against it. Rejected naming a target year. A yes for 2035 and a yes for 2060 are genuinely different, but the disagreement candidates actually split on first is binding date versus none; pinning a year would make a no out of every candidate who wants a deadline at a different date, which is worse. The year belongs in each candidate's summary and quote beneath the proposition. Rejected the double-barreled charge. A candidate who wants fossil generation ended through an adjustable regulatory target rather than a fixed statutory date is a legitimate no here, and their summary will say so; per the mechanism rule, the deadline is the policy, not a bundled extra.

proposition: Lower the legal limits on what factories, landfills, and utilities may release into local water, even if that raises costs and household bills.
yesMeans: Facilities may release less into local water; costs and household bills rise.
noMeans: Facilities may release the same as now; costs and household bills hold.
scope: All levels except school boards. Congress and EPA set national floors under the Clean Water and Safe Drinking Water Acts; states write, enforce, and may tighten most discharge permits; counties and cities act through the discharge standards of their own water and sewer utilities, industrial-waste and pretreatment ordinances, landfill and siting conditions, and formal comment or appeal on state permits.
changedBecause: Accepted three of the plain reviewer's points. (1) Free-lunch valence: agreeing now names its counterweight — higher costs and household bills — so a no has a stated reason instead of reading as "for more pollution." (2) Asymmetric glosses: both sides now state the same two consequences, one direction each. (3) Permit literacy: "than their current permits set" is gone; "lower the legal limits on what X may release" needs no knowledge of how permits work. Also narrowed to water, because this issue is defined as water, land, and waste — air belongs to climate-energy — which answers the "which pollution type" objection. Rejected three. Splitting factories, landfills, and utilities into separate propositions breaks the one-proposition-per-issue rule, and the specific worry behind it (a municipal utility passing costs to ratepayers) is now carried by the cost clause, so a voter who objects on those grounds has a no to vote. Quantifying "tighter" was rejected: a proposition fixes direction, and any number would be arbitrary and meaningless across a city council and a US senator. "The officeholder cannot do it" was rejected as a wording problem — that is what the scope field is for, and local offices do act here through their own utilities' standards, waste ordinances, siting conditions, and permit comments. The reviewer's suggested wording was not adopted verbatim: "even if that raises their costs and customer bills" tacks the cost onto the facilities alone, while "raises costs and household bills" states it as the voter experiences it, and "large industrial, waste, and utility facilities" is more abstract than the three plain nouns.

proposition: Shift a larger share of transportation money from building and widening roads to public transit, sidewalks, and bike lanes.
yesMeans: Transit, sidewalks, and bike lanes get more; road building gets less.
noMeans: Road building keeps or grows its share; transit, sidewalks, and bike lanes do not.
scope: City, county, state, and federal. Each level splits a transportation budget between road capacity and transit/walking/biking: councils over street funds and local transit, counties over roads and transit authorities, states over DOT programs and formula splits, Congress over the highway-versus-transit share of federal funds. Not school district — a school board's only transportation decision is bus service, so this proposition does not apply to trustee races and the issue's SCHOOL_DISTRICT level should not be scored against it.
changedBecause: All three reviewers passed it unchanged.

proposition: Allow any registered voter to vote by mail without giving a reason, rather than only those meeting conditions such as age, illness, or travel.
yesMeans: Any registered voter may request a mail ballot
noMeans: Only voters meeting set conditions may request a mail ballot
scope: State legislatures set who may vote by mail; Congress can set a national floor. County election officials run mail balloting but do not set eligibility, so city council and school board candidates have no decision here, only a stated view. Where a state already allows it, yes means keeping it open to all and no means restoring conditions.
changedBecause:
Accepted three things. (1) Dropped "loosening"/"tightening" entirely. The left reviewer is right that "loosening" is the opponents' adjective and that its pairing with "tightening" hands the reader a free push toward no; the right reviewer conceded the same tilt. The new glosses are mechanically parallel and end on the same words. (2) Un-bundled the stem. The plain reviewer's strongest point stands: favoring more early-voting sites while opposing no-excuse mail ballots is one of the most common real positions, so the old sentence was unanswerable for those candidates, and no single verbatim quote could ever cover mail voting plus hours plus registration — the extractor would have had to invent a stance to satisfy the evidence rule. Kept the one change candidates speak to on the record. (3) Replaced "beyond what current law allows" with the actual baseline (age, illness, travel), so a voter who does not know their state's rules can still tell what they are answering.

Rejected the left reviewer's rewrite: it swaps "allows" for "provides" and keeps all three changes in one sentence, fixing the smallest defect and leaving the largest, and its no gloss still merges status quo with rollback.

Rejected the plain reviewer's split into three propositions — the brief is one per issue — and took its own fallback. Also rejected its demand that the stem name a cost or countervailing concern: writing an argument into the stem imports one side's case. The fix for "yes looks obviously correct" is that no is now a stated rule rather than the absence of one, so both answers name a policy someone holds.

Avoided "no-excuse absentee" and "universal mail voting"; both are camp terms. "Without giving a reason" is the literal mechanism.

One limit is unavoidable with a binary: a candidate who would narrow current eligibility and one who would keep it both answer no. The wording at least pins no to a concrete rule instead of "keeping or tightening."

proposition: Add sexual orientation and gender identity to the categories covered by laws banning discrimination in housing, employment, and businesses open to the public.
yesMeans: Extend existing anti-discrimination law to cover sexual orientation and gender identity.
noMeans: Keep the categories that anti-discrimination law currently covers as they are.
scope: All levels. Congress can amend federal civil rights and fair housing law; state legislatures can add these categories to state law; city and county councils can pass local ordinances where state law does not preempt them. Note that federal employment law already covers these categories after Bostock (2020), so the change is largest in housing and public accommodations, and in the states and localities with no such law.
changedBecause: All three reviewers passed it unchanged.

proposition: Bar government agencies from using race or sex as a factor when hiring employees or awarding public contracts.
yesMeans: Agencies must decide hiring and contracts without weighing race or sex.
noMeans: Agencies may weigh race or sex when deciding hiring and contracts.
scope: Federal, state, county, city, and school-district bodies — any government that hires staff or awards contracts. Applies wherever the jurisdiction runs its own personnel or procurement system.
changedBecause:
Three changes, and two refusals.

Changed 1 — dropped public college admissions. The left reviewer is right on the law: SFFA v. Harvard (2023) already bars race-conscious admissions, so leaving admissions in would make "disagree" an endorsement of something currently unconstitutional. That breaks hard rule 5 — the no side must be a position a real candidate can hold and defend today. Public hiring and public contracting are still genuinely live and lawful in most states, so both answers survive there. Admissions after SFFA (percentage plans, socioeconomic criteria, how race may appear in an applicant's own essay) is a separate proposition and should be drafted as one.

Changed 2 — fixed the "still" asymmetry in the glosses. The left reviewer caught a real defect: "may still be considered" implies an unexamined practice continuing rather than a rule someone affirmatively defends. Both glosses are now the same grammatical object — a rule about what agencies may or must do, same length, same structure, no time direction in either.

Changed 3 — dropped "government agencies" ambiguity by dropping what caused it. Both the right and overlap reviewers noted agencies do not admit students. With admissions gone, "government agencies" is exactly right: agencies do hire and do award contracts, and the phrase reaches federal, state, and local alike, which "state and local government" would not.

Refused 1 — I did not add purpose language to the disagree gloss. The left reviewer wants "to counter documented discrimination and widen access." That is a motive clause, and hard rule 4 forbids describing the goal rather than the mechanism. The right reviewer independently flagged this as the exact spot where the item would leak: give one side its rationale and the other side only a rule, and you have handed one answer its best argument inside the instrument. Note that both reviewers pointed at the same clause from opposite directions — the left calling its absence a bias, the right calling its presence one. That is the signal that neither side gets it.

Refused 2 — I kept race and sex bundled. All three reviewers flagged the compound. I accept the cost and keep it, because this is how the question is actually put to candidates: Prop 209, Michigan Prop 2, Washington I-200, and California Prop 16 all bundle race and sex in public employment and public contracting, and candidates take positions on the bundle, not the halves. Splitting would produce two propositions with near-identical stance records and would misdescribe what anyone has actually said. Splitting the arenas was the more defensible cut, and I made that one instead by removing admissions. A candidate who backs women-owned business goals but not race-conscious hiring will land in NO_STATED_POSITION, which is the correct outcome under the guide's own rules — better an honest blank than a stance inferred from one half.

On the residual tilt the right reviewer volunteered: "as a factor" polls harder against the practice than "affirmative action programs" does. There is no neutral term here — "affirmative action" tilts the other way just as far. "Factor" is the operative language in both SFFA and the ballot-measure family, so it is the wording both sides use in the fight itself, which is the closest thing to neutral available.

On overlap: confirmed clear. The LGBTQ+ proposition adds sexual orientation and gender identity to protected categories in private housing, jobs, and public accommodations. This one restricts government's use of two long-covered characteristics in its own decisions — different actor, different mechanism, different characteristics, and neither answer implies the other. The right reviewer's caution about post-Bostock "sex" sweeping in gender identity does not bite here, because the proposition governs preference decisions by a government employer and contracting body, not the scope of a nondiscrimination statute.

proposition: Require companies to file results of testing for bias with a government agency before using AI to decide who gets a job, loan, or apartment.
yesMeans: A government agency receives the test results before the system is used.
noMeans: A company decides its own testing, and answers for problems only afterward.
scope: Federal, state, and city/county. Cities (New York) and states (Colorado, Illinois) have passed versions of this; Congress and federal agencies can set a national rule. Any level that regulates employers, lenders, or landlords can act.
changedBecause:
Accepted the double-barrel fix as the main change. The old sentence bundled "must test" (almost nobody argues for untested systems) with "must file with government before use" (the actually contested part), so agreement on the easy half dragged the hard half along. The proposition is now only the pre-use filing requirement — a candidate who wants companies to test but opposes a government filing regime now has a clean no, and that position is written into noMeans.

Accepted the vagueness fix, partly. "Test" alone did not say test for what, so a voter could not tell what they were agreeing to. Named it as testing for bias, which is what every enacted law of this kind measures. Rejected the left reviewer's "for discriminatory outcomes": "discriminatory" carries a legal finding of wrongdoing and states the conclusion the test is meant to check, which tilts toward yes. "Testing for bias" describes the instrument, not a verdict — the same way testing for lead does not presume lead.

Accepted the asymmetry fix. Both clauses now name an actor and a timing and run to the same length; neither side is stated as an absence. Rejected the left reviewer's claim that repeating "government" is a thumb on the scale — the government's role is the entire contested content of this proposition, and naming it plainly on both sides is what makes the choice legible. Rejected the plain reviewer's suggested wording for a different reason: "answer only if a problem surfaces later" makes the no side sound negligent.

Kept the three domains bundled. Both reviewers flagged it, both at low severity. Hiring, lending, and housing are the standard statutory triple for high-stakes automated decisions, no real candidate splits them, and unbundling would cost three propositions to gain almost nothing.

Kept "a government agency" rather than naming a level, so the same proposition compares a city council candidate and a senator, each answering for the agency they would actually direct. The scope field carries the detail.

proposition: Raise total U.S. military spending above its current level, rather than holding it steady or reducing it.
yesMeans: Backs a larger military budget than today's.
noMeans: Backs a military budget kept flat or smaller.
scope: Federal only. Congress appropriates military spending and the president proposes the budget. State and local officials have no authority here; a mayor or state legislator may hold a view but cannot act on it, so expect NO_STATED_POSITION for most non-federal offices.
changedBecause: All three reviewers passed it unchanged.

proposition: Allow more than one home per lot in areas now zoned for single-family homes only.
yesMeans: Change the rules so more homes are allowed on those lots
noMeans: Keep the rules so one home is allowed on those lots
scope: Local only. City councils hold the zoning authority this describes; county commissioners hold it in states where counties zone unincorporated land (in Texas and several others they largely do not). School boards do not set zoning, so trustees will usually be NO_STATED_POSITION here even though the issue is masked to their level for campus siting.
changedBecause: All three reviewers passed it unchanged.
